Without such coordination, increases in peak demand may require costly grid upgrades, increase electricity prices, and increase the risk of outages or degraded service. This ResStock™ (Reyna et al. 2025) measure assigns one EV and an L2 charger to each occupied dwelling unit model in the baseline scenario. All existing units with level 1 (L1) chargers are upgraded to L2. By modeling widespread adoption of EVs and chargers, ResStock users can combine models from both the baseline and the measure to create their own unique EV saturation scenarios. This allows nuanced scenarios in which only segments of households adopt EVs or shift their charging load. Such a method can be used to model EV and charger adoption scenarios and examine the resulting energy and power impacts on the residential building sector. The simultaneous charging of EVs at multiple dwelling units in this measure can also quantify the potential stress that a local electric grid may incur during peak charging hours. 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Technology Summary 2.1 Introduction to Electric Vehicles in ResStock EVs are an increasingly important component of residential energy demand, with charging behavior often correlated with other household loads due to shared occupancy and behavioral patterns. The current ResStock baseline reflects 2023 EV saturation levels, which corresponds to a small number of representative dwelling unit models with EVs (1.05% of all datapoints). For each EV-owning dwelling unit, ResStock assigns specific vehicle properties, driving behavior, and charging behavior dependent on location, demographics (income and tenure), or occupancy – factors that also influence other household load profiles. While the baseline includes a limited number of EVs, ResStock’s EV measures enable scenario analysis of future adoption and charging patterns. This measure comprises two components: adoption of an EV and adoption of an L2 charger. EV charging power in ResStock depends on the vehicle charger type, while EV charging demand depends on characteristics of the EV and driver behavior. When an EV is assigned to a dwelling unit in ResStock, the characteristics of the vehicle, driving behavior, and charging behavior are predetermined in the sampling routine, using distributions sourced from the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) and other datasets (Speake et al. 2025). ResStock leverages physics-based modeling, where high-level EV and driving behavior ResStock inputs are translated to EnergyPlus inputs to model the charging energy demand of an individual dwelling unit, as shown in Figure 1. The ResStock baseline is consistent with EV saturations from 2023, which corresponds to a small number of representative models with EVs. The ResStock EV characteristics that inform the energy model and influence the charging energy demand include the (1) EV battery/vehicle type, (2) annual vehicle miles traveled (VMT), and (3) at-home charging fraction.
